topic: How to give feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings
scope_note: Workplace feedback between peers or from a lead to a colleague: what makes it usable (specific behaviour, effect, next step, timing). Not performance-review systems, not formal appraisal, not coaching theory, no statistics.

facts.statement: A comment changes what someone does only if they can tell which action to repeat or change; general praise or general criticism leaves them with a feeling but no action to aim at.
facts.caveat: This is the working explanation drawn from feedback research and practice, not a single measured law. Say it as why vague comments tend to leave behaviour where it was, not that they never work.
facts.reference_hint: Hattie and Timperley, The Power of Feedback (Review of Educational Research, 2007)

facts.statement: Research on feedback shows its effect on performance varies a lot: on average it helps, but some feedback has no effect or makes performance worse, so feedback is not automatically useful just because it was given.
facts.caveat: Based on a large meta-analysis of feedback interventions, mostly from lab and some field settings. Say 'feedback does not automatically help', and do not quote proportions.
facts.reference_hint: Kluger and DeNisi, meta-analysis of feedback interventions (Psychological Bulletin, 1996)

facts.statement: Feedback aimed at the task and at how to do it better is generally more useful than feedback aimed at the person, such as general praise or a judgement of who they are.
facts.caveat: A synthesis of education and some work research, with exceptions depending on context. Say 'tends to be more useful'.
facts.reference_hint: Hattie and Timperley (2007), The Power of Feedback

facts.statement: Behaviour is what a person visibly did or said, which another person could have seen or heard; a character or personality label such as 'careless' or 'disorganised' is a conclusion drawn from behaviour, not the behaviour itself.

Describing what you observed gives the other person something specific to recognise and respond to, while a comment about their character tends to prompt defensiveness and gives them nothing concrete to change.
facts.caveat: Widely taught by practitioners and consistent with the research on person-focused feedback, but how people react depends on trust and on how the comment is said. Say 'tends to'.

facts.statement: Naming the effect of the behaviour on other people or on the work shows the person why it matters, and lets them see the consequence they may not have noticed.
facts.caveat: Taught as a core part of behaviour-focused feedback structures; it is practitioner consensus rather than a separately tested ingredient. The effect should be something actually seen or known, not a guess about what others felt.

facts.statement: Specific goals tend to lead to better performance than vague goals such as 'do your best', which is a reason to end feedback with one concrete thing to try next time rather than a general wish to improve.
facts.caveat: This is established for goal setting in general and applied here by analogy to a feedback next step. Say it as a reason, not as proof about feedback conversations specifically.
facts.reference_hint: Locke and Latham, goal-setting theory (American Psychologist, 2002)

facts.statement: A next step that is agreed in a two-way conversation, where the other person can add context and shape what they will try, is more likely to be owned and carried out than one that is simply handed over.
facts.caveat: Common coaching and management guidance, supported by general research on participation in goal setting but not a firm rule for every situation. Say 'is more likely'.

facts.statement: Feedback is easier to use when it is given soon after the moment it is about, because both people still remember the specifics and the person can try the change at the next chance.
facts.caveat: Research on immediate versus delayed feedback is mixed for some tasks, and a short pause can help when emotions are high or privacy is needed. Say 'soon', not 'immediately', and give no time limit.

facts.statement: Memory of the details of an event fades, and it fades fastest soon afterwards, so the specifics of what someone did become harder to describe accurately as time passes.
facts.reference_hint: Ebbinghaus (1885), on the shape of forgetting

facts.statement: Specific positive feedback, which names what someone did well and why it worked, helps them repeat it, while general praise feels good but does not say what to keep doing.
facts.caveat: Follows from the findings on task-focused feedback. The point is specificity, not that praise is bad; kind words are fine and are better when they name the behaviour.

facts.statement: Specificity is a separate matter from tone: feedback can be specific and warm, or specific and critical, and either can be vague.
facts.caveat: A framing point drawn from the same research and practice, not a measured result.

facts.statement: Situation-Behavior-Impact, usually shortened to SBI, is a feedback structure developed and taught by the Center for Creative Leadership: describe the situation, the behaviour observed, and the impact it had.
facts.reference_hint: Center for Creative Leadership, Situation-Behavior-Impact (SBI) feedback tool

facts.statement: SBI is one of several behaviour-focused feedback structures, and no single structure has been shown to be the only valid one; what they share is describing observed behaviour and its effect.
facts.caveat: The lesson stays model-neutral. If SBI is named at all, name it as one option among several.

terms.definition: What a person visibly did or said, which someone else could have seen or heard.
What the behaviour caused for other people or for the work, as actually seen or known.
One concrete, forward-looking thing to try next time, ideally agreed in conversation.
General praise, general criticism or a hint that gives no specific behaviour to repeat or change.

not_claimed: Any percentage or ratio about feedback, such as 'X percent of employees' or a fixed positive-to-negative ratio like five to one as settled.
That the feedback sandwich (praise, criticism, praise) is proven to work or proven to fail; the evidence is not settled and the lesson does not give a verdict.
That one named model, including SBI, is the only correct way to give feedback.
That praise or positive feedback is harmful; the point is specificity, not tone.
Any learning-styles claim, or retention percentages by how information is delivered.
That feedback must be given immediately or within a fixed time.
Any quote, saying or study presented as real research that is not named in this sheet.
